What Is a Mandala? Meaning, History and How They're Used

By Super Mandala Lab · October 28, 2026

A mandala is a design organized around a center, usually inside a circle, with its parts repeating evenly around that center. The word comes from Sanskrit, where it is most often translated as "circle." In Hindu and Buddhist traditions a mandala is much more than a pattern: it is a sacred diagram, used in ritual and meditation to represent the universe or a realm centered on a deity.

Today the word is also used loosely for almost any circular, symmetrical design, from coloring pages to tattoos to laser-cut wall art. This guide covers both meanings, so you can enjoy making mandalas while understanding where they come from.

Where the word comes from

"Mandala" (मण्डल) appears in early Sanskrit texts, where it can mean a circle, a disc or a circular arrangement. The ten books of the Rigveda, one of the oldest Hindu scriptures, are themselves called mandalas. Over time the word came to name a specific kind of sacred image: a carefully arranged diagram with a center, boundaries and directions.

Mandalas in Hindu and Buddhist practice

In both traditions a mandala maps a sacred space. The center is the most important point, and everything else is arranged in rings and directions around it. Practitioners may visualize moving from the outer edge toward the center as part of meditation.

  • Hindu tradition. Closely related diagrams called yantras use precise geometry, often triangles, petals and squares around a central point called the bindu. The Sri Yantra, built from interlocking triangles, is one of the best known.
  • Buddhist tradition. Many Tibetan Buddhist mandalas show a square palace with a gate on each of its four sides, set inside rings of circles. The palace holds a central deity, and the surrounding figures and colors carry specific meanings within the teaching.

Tibetan sand mandalas

One of the most striking traditions is the Tibetan sand mandala. Monks lay colored sand, grain by grain, using narrow metal funnels, often working for days or weeks on a single design. When it is finished and the ceremony is complete, the mandala is swept away, and the sand is often poured into flowing water. The dismantling is part of the practice: it is a reminder that everything is impermanent.

The parts of a mandala

Whatever the tradition, most mandalas share a few structural ideas, and these are the same ideas that make a mandala satisfying to draw:

  • A center. A dot, a small circle or a flower that everything grows from.
  • Rings. Concentric bands that separate one layer of the design from the next.
  • Radial symmetry. The circle is divided into equal slices, and each element repeats in every slice. Many designs also mirror within each slice.
  • A boundary. An outer circle or square that closes the design.

Carl Jung and the mandala

In the twentieth century the Swiss psychiatrist Carl Jung brought mandalas to a Western audience. He drew mandalas himself and wrote about them as images of wholeness that appear in many cultures and in the drawings of his patients. His writing is a big part of why mandalas are popular in Western art and journaling today.

Circular designs in other cultures

Many cultures have made circular, radially symmetric designs, such as the rose windows of Gothic cathedrals and the geometric star patterns of Islamic art. They share the geometry of a mandala, but each has its own history and meaning, and they are not mandalas in the religious sense.

Mandalas today

Outside religious practice, mandala-style designs are everywhere: adult coloring books, wall art, tattoos, henna, embroidery, stained glass, stickers and laser- or plasma-cut metal. People enjoy drawing and coloring them because the repetition is calming and the symmetry makes even simple shapes look finished.

If you make or sell mandala art, it is worth remembering that for many people these designs are sacred. Avoid copying specific religious mandalas for decoration, and describe your own designs as mandala-inspired patterns rather than as religious objects.
